title: "No formal assessment of blinding integrity...was conducted" Psychedelic Research Can't Go Back in Time, Can It?
subtitle: Assessing the blinding is crucial.
text:
This is The Frontier Psychiatrists! It is a newsletter, edited and (often) authored by Owen Scott Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, which reviews the science of human health, and does so with a satirical tone to prevent us all from dying of boredom. It’s like David Foster Wallace both got to the point, and used his Amherst College education to explain medical science instead of just griping about regrettable 7 Night Caribbean Cruises.

This past week, we have another phase 2b psilocybin trial authored by Ross et. al. published1 this paper:

Psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy for depression and anxiety associated with life-threatening illness: A phase 2b randomized controlled trial

This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with an open-label extension assessed the efficacy of psilocybin versus niacin/placebo combined with psychotherapy to alleviate depression and/or anxiety in patients with life-threatening illness.

And, if it's 2025, the thing everyone's going to want to know is… “was their functional unblinding.” Spoiler alert: they didn’t even check. It is hard to argue that a study is double blind if you don’t know if the blinding held up. It is a bit like a child claiming their room is “totally clean” while begging to play more video games. Just taking my son’s word for it, when extra iPad time with his friends on Minecraft is on the line, is probably unwise. So, too, with hard to blind clinical trials using non-consciousness-altering substances for “active” placebo groups.

This study, sponsored by Usona Institute, is, notwithstanding blinding issues, a well-structured clinical trial. The individuals in the trial were adults, and all of them had a life-threatening illness. The study was conducted in Australia at two palliative care departments in two major hospitals in Melbourne:

Adults aged 18–80 with a life-threatening illness and clinically significant depression and/or anxiety.

The investigators used either 25 mg of psilocybin as the active agent or 100 mg of niacin as the “active placebo.” I've previously written about the use of psilocybin in clinical trials2, here. A nice review of “active controls” in psychedelic trials is here.3

The primary outcome was:

the change in depression and anxiety symptoms, assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), from baseline to 6–7 weeks post-dose.

A scale commonly used in hospital settings. The intervention worked:

Thirty-five participants (mean age 56.0; 54.3 % female) were randomized (psilocybin: n = 17; placebo: n = 18). At 6–7 weeks, psilocybin produced significantly greater reductions in HADS depression (B = –2.49; P = .02; d = 1.12), …compared to placebo.

That d=1.12 is a large effect size…

However, a few items of note in a relatively small trial. This study involved a blinded, randomized dose comparison of dose one followed by an active dose two—everyone crossed over to psilocybin. There was no difference in the crossover from placebo to the second dose, only between niacin and psilocybin in dose one.

In part, this is because there was a sufficient positive response in both the placebo and active groups, making further change less likely. Another issue is that the sample size would be too small to detect a difference in another comparison, as the authors concede. However, another way to look at this trial is that in the “cross over” only group, there was no difference between the placebo and psilocybin. This wasn’t a prespecified endpoint, and it’s not a fair comparison in this trial, but it seems worth evaluating in subsequent trials—this methodology has been very fruitful in, for example, clozapine research4.

This is a phase 2b study—so they aren’t expected to answer every question. These studies are designed to follow up on phase 2a studies and get the following tasks done:

The objectives of Phase 2b trials shift slightly toward confirming dosage, determining optimal administration methods, and evaluating overall therapeutic effects in a broader group of subjects. They are also utilized to uncover any unforeseen side effects that may arise at different dosages.

So it's not that you're mandated to produce sample sizes that are larger than would be reasonable at that phase, nor are you attempting to answer every question. Phase 2b studies are conducted to ensure that the Phase 3 trial has the necessary data to answer the crucial question of whether the treatment is safe and effective in the evaluated illnesses. However, it is the case that all studies are published long after they are planned. And when this study, and most other studies, were planned, we didn't live through the FDA AdCom for MDMA, where functional unblinding was such a pertinent issue. This study missed its enrollment numbers because it was carried out, in part, during COVID-19!

only 35 were enrolled due to funding and time constraints (including delays and logistical difficulties during the COVID pandemic), resulting in an underpowered study despite statistically significant outcomes.

This is both predictable, but it’s tempting to review studies in the era in which their results are published, not in the era when they were planned and enrollment took place. This would be an error! We have learned, since then, that functional unblinding will be THE issue on which these compounds and their administration protocols are judged.

It’s also true that no matter what your task is in a clinical trial, imaging the minds of future readers, even obnoxious know-it-alls like Owen Muir, M.D., is the business you are in. Imagining the audience is crucial, regardless of how critical, in the design and drafting of manuscripts. Please answer the questions they have prominently! Dear psychedelic researchers, if you take nothing else away from this newsletter, which is cheering for your success, it's to include in your manuscripts the answers to our questions in the most obvious way possible.

These authors demonstrated that psilocybin may offer hope for human depression at the end of life, and I look forward to the phase III trial. However, don’t skimp on preserving the blind!
